newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union threatens strikes over working hours.
newsitem.headline: German union threatens strikes over working hours.

text.p: The largest German trade union, IG Metall, on Wednesday said it was ready to back strikes by workers in a row over working hours, threatening a new round of industrial unrest.

The union said that, if needed, it would back strikes among its 2.7 million members in favour of an early retirement scheme which it has proposed to boost job creation in Germany's large but struggling metal and engineering sectors.
"Work hours cuts must be put in place by late 1998 to early 1999 as part of the fight against unemployment," the union said in a statement issued during a meeting of its main board.

"If necessary, this proposal (on early retirement) can be pushed through with strikes," IG Metall said. The union said at the weekend that strikes to secure a general 32-hour week were possible on that issue, too.

Engineering employers federation Gesamtmetall, which had been due to meet IG Metall last weekend to discuss the retirement plan before the union called off the talks, said the strike threat was "absolutely irresponsible".
It added that it would put up "full resistance" to any moves to cut working hours.
Germany, with unemployment stuck at 4.5 million, has recently been hit by a number of protests by workers anxious to keep their jobs.
Apart from demonstrations by coalminers and steel-workers, there has also been widespread labour opposition to sick pay and other welfare cuts introduced late last year.

IG Metall and other major unions made it clear at an employment conference last week that they saw reduced working hours and overtime as the main ways to reach a previously-agreed goal between unions, employers and the government of halving joblessness by 2000.

Equally clear has been the opposition of the Bonn government and employer groups to such measures. They argue that they would only make German labour more expensive and thus increase the long-term risk of unemployment.
Economics Minister Guenther Rexrodt said on German radio that IG Metall's proposal for a 32-hour week was "an old chestnut" that was completely unworkable.
But he also rejected a proposal made on Monday by the BDA, Germany's main employers federation, for the introduction of state subsidies to create a new layer of low-wage work.

While Gesamtmetall had been willing to discuss the early retirement scheme proposed by IG Metall, it insisted the plan as it stood was too expensive. It puts the cost to firms at 210,000 marks ($121,000) per worker involved in the scheme.
The proposed model would allow workers effectively to retire five years early while retaining full pension entitlements.

Under the scheme, 55-year-old workers would receive 85 percent of their full salary for the last 10 years of their working life. They would then work full-time for five years before being released at the age of 60.
Yet more controversial was a proposal by IG Metall chief Klaus Zwickel under which the working week in the metal and engineering sectors would be reduced from the current 35 hours to 32 hours.
While Zwickel acknowledged for the first time that such a move would also necessitate a drop in salaries, he insisted wages should not fall proportionately to the cut in hours.
Gesamtmetall, rejecting any general move to shortened work hours, in turn proposed a so-called working time "corridor" laying down working weeks of between 30 and 40 hours.

Such contracts would be agreed by firms with individual workers but, marking a crucial difference to the union plan, the contracts would be on the basis that employees were then paid only according to the number of hours they worked.

A spokeswoman for IG Metall said it was making no comment on the Gesamtmetall proposal, saying it was merely a "reaction to our (plan)". She said no further information had emerged from the union board meeting, where Zwickel was due to present in full his 32-hour week proposal to other board members.
